Chapter 2: The ‘Jobs to Be Done’ Theory—A New Lens for Understanding Customers.
Let’s dive into a fresh way of looking at why people choose the products and services they do. The "Jobs to Be Done" theory gives us a really powerful perspective here.
Instead of thinking about customers as just buyers, this theory asks us to imagine people "hiring" a product to help them achieve something meaningful in their lives. Think of it like this—when someone buys a drill, they’re not really after the drill itself.
What they actually want is a hole in the wall. But even that isn’t the whole story. Maybe they want to hang a family photo, to make their house feel a little more like home.
So, the real "job" isn’t owning a drill—it’s making progress in their lives, in a way that matters to them.
This approach helps us move past old-school categories and market segments. Instead, we’re looking at the moments and situations that trigger a need—the real-life challenges or opportunities that people face.
The "job" is all about the context, the struggle, and that deep-down drive for progress.
There are a few key ideas that make this theory come alive.
First, a "job" is always tied to a specific situation. It’s not just a vague want—it’s a particular challenge or chance that pops up in someone’s life.
Second, the "job" stays pretty stable over time, even as products change. People have always wanted to communicate across distances, right? The tools have evolved—from handwritten letters, to telephones, to instant messaging—but the core job hasn’t really changed.
And third, understanding the real job takes empathy and genuine curiosity. It means watching how people act, listening to their stories, and picking up on those hidden motivations that drive their choices.
So, how do you actually use this theory? You’ve got to start seeing the world through your customers’ eyes. Go beyond what people say they like or dislike—try to uncover what they’re really hoping to accomplish.
Ask yourself: What is this person trying to do, right now? What’s getting in their way? And what would make them feel like they’ve truly made progress?
Here’s a great real-world example. A fast-food chain noticed a surprising trend: a lot of customers were buying milkshakes in the morning. Their usual research couldn’t explain it. But when they watched and talked to these customers, they discovered something interesting—people were "hiring" milkshakes to make their long commutes a bit more enjoyable and to keep them full until lunch.
The milkshake wasn’t just a treat. For these commuters, it was the perfect answer to a very specific job.
That insight changed everything. Instead of just creating a better-tasting milkshake, the company made tweaks so their morning milkshakes did the commute job even better. And guess what? Sales went up.
The magic was in understanding the real job, not just the product itself.
So, the "Jobs to Be Done" theory gives us a practical way to see what really drives customer choices. It’s about focusing on the progress people want to make, not just the features you offer or the market segment you’re targeting.
When you look at the world this way, you can create solutions that fit beautifully into people’s lives—and you’re much more likely to spot the innovations that will actually succeed.
